expectedText:
NEUTRAL REFERENCE / EMPLOYMENT VERIFICATION POLICY
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme, Inc.

REFERENCE REQUEST OVERVIEW
Beta Corp Hiring Manager has asked Acme, Inc. for information about Jordan Alex Lee's former employment. This document sets out the California legal framework that applies to how Acme, Inc. responds to a reference or verification request — it states the law and does not tell Acme, Inc. what to say in any particular case.

BLACKLISTING PROHIBITION
California makes it a crime for a former employer, or its agent or officer, to prevent or attempt to prevent a former employee from obtaining employment elsewhere by misrepresentation. If Acme, Inc. communicates with Beta Corp Hiring Manager about Jordan Alex Lee's former employment, that communication is the kind of act this statute reaches. A violation is a misdemeanor.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Any person, or agent or officer thereof, who, after having discharged an employee from the service of such person or after an employee has voluntarily left such service, by any misrepresentation prevents or attempts to prevent the former employee from obtaining employment, is guilty of a misdemeanor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1050 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1050.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a blacklisting prohibition of this kind exists in at least one jurisdiction — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular employer-employee relationship. Coverage turns on the word “misrepresentation”: the statute reaches false or misleading communications intended to prevent re-employment, not merely negative-but-truthful ones, a line its companion provision (Labor Code section 1053) draws directly by carving out truthful statements furnished on request. Whether any given communication crosses that line is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1050); no additional independent source was found for this.

TRUTHFUL STATEMENT ON REQUEST
The same chapter of California's Labor Code that makes blacklisting a crime also protects a truthful statement about why Jordan Alex Lee's employment with Acme, Inc. ended, when that statement is given upon a special request for it — such as a request from Beta Corp Hiring Manager. The statute adds an evidentiary rule of its own: if the statement conveys information through a mark, sign, code, or other means different from what its words say, or if information of that kind is given without having been specially requested, that fact is itself prima facie evidence of a violation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Nothing in this chapter shall prevent an employer or an agent, employee, superintendent or manager thereof from furnishing, upon special request therefor, a truthful statement concerning the reason for the discharge of an employee or why an employee voluntarily left the service of the employer. If such statement furnishes any mark, sign, or other means conveying information different from that expressed by words therein, such fact, or the fact that such statement or other means of furnishing information was given without a special request therefor is prima facie evidence of a violation of sections 1050 to 1053."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1053 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1053.)
  Known gap: This clause corrects a common mislabeling: Labor Code section 1053 is not itself the criminal-penalty provision for blacklisting — the misdemeanor penalty is written into section 1050. Section 1053 instead operates as a safe harbor, affirmatively permitting a truthful, specially-requested statement about the reason for separation, while also creating a specific evidentiary trap for coded or unsolicited signals. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a safe-harbor and evidentiary rule of this kind exists — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reference request. Whether a specific communication was “specially requested,” or used a “mark, sign, or other means” conveying different information, are fact-specific questions this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1053); no additional independent source was found for this.

CIVIL TREBLE-DAMAGES REMEDY
Beyond misdemeanor criminal exposure, a person, or agent or officer, who violates the blacklisting provisions is also civilly liable in a private lawsuit for treble damages — three times the actual damages of the party aggrieved. If Jordan Alex Lee believes a communication from Acme, Inc. to Beta Corp Hiring Manager crossed that line, this civil remedy can be pursued without first establishing criminal liability.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "In addition to and apart from the criminal penalty provided any person or agent or officer thereof, who violates any provision of sections 1050 to 1052, inclusive, is liable to the party aggrieved, in a civil action, for treble damages. Such civil action may be brought by such aggrieved person or his assigns, or successors in interest, without first establishing any criminal liability under this article."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1054 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1054.)
  Known gap: The civil treble-damages remedy applies, by its own text, to violations of sections 1050 through 1052 — not section 1053, which (as the surrounding clause explains) is a safe-harbor provision rather than a prohibition. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a private treble-damages remedy for this kind of misconduct exists in at least one jurisdiction — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular dispute, and not a calculation of what damages, if any, would be available in a specific case. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1054); no additional independent source was found for this.

QUALIFIED PRIVILEGE FOR EMPLOYER COMMUNICATIONS
Separately, California's Civil Code gives Acme, Inc. a qualified legal privilege for a communication about Jordan Alex Lee's job performance or qualifications. The privilege covers a communication made without malice, based on credible evidence, by Acme, Inc. to Beta Corp Hiring Manager when Acme, Inc. reasonably believes Beta Corp Hiring Manager is a prospective employer of Jordan Alex Lee and the communication is made at Beta Corp Hiring Manager's request. The same provision also lets Acme, Inc. state, without malice, whether it would rehire Jordan Alex Lee, and whether a decision not to rehire rests on a determination that Jordan Alex Lee engaged in sexual harassment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "In a communication, without malice, to a person interested therein, (1) by one who is also interested, or (2) by one who stands in such a relation to the person interested as to afford a reasonable ground for supposing the motive for the communication to be innocent, or (3) who is requested by the person interested to give the information. This subdivision applies to and includes a communication concerning the job performance or qualifications of an applicant for employment, based upon credible evidence, made without malice, by a current or former employer of the applicant to, and upon request of, one whom the employer reasonably believes is a prospective employer of the applicant. ... This subdivision authorizes a current or former employer, or the employer’s agent, to answer, without malice, whether or not the employer would rehire a current or former employee and whether the decision to not rehire is based upon the employer’s determination that the former employee engaged in sexual harassment."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 47(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=47.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a qualified reference privilege of this kind exists — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular communication. The privilege is conditional, not absolute: by its own terms it applies only “without malice,” so a communication made with malice falls outside it. Independent case law addressing exactly what conduct defeats this privilege was not verified for this clause: CourtListener research for that case law was rate-limited during drafting and was not pursued further past that point, so that gap is disclosed here rather than filled with an unverified case citation. Whether any particular communication is privileged, or was made with malice, is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 47(c)); no additional independent source was found for this.

NO STATUTORY MANDATE FOR A NEUTRAL-REFERENCE FORMAT
California law does not require Acme, Inc. to limit what it tells Beta Corp Hiring Manager to only Jordan Alex Lee's dates of employment and job title. A strict “neutral reference” policy of that kind is a risk-management practice some employers choose to adopt — it is not a rule California statute imposes. Nor does the statute discussed above set a specific deadline for responding to Beta Corp Hiring Manager's request, or require the request to be in writing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Nothing in this chapter shall prevent an employer or an agent, employee, superintendent or manager thereof from furnishing, upon special request therefor, a truthful statement concerning the reason for the discharge of an employee or why an employee voluntarily left the service of the employer."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1053 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1053.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of what these specific provisions do and do not require — not an exhaustive survey of every California statute that could conceivably touch reference requests, and not a claim about which state's law governs any particular employer's practice. A “neutral reference” policy limiting responses to dates and title is a widely adopted risk-management practice precisely because it avoids the fact-specific line-drawing the statutes above require — but adopting it is a choice, not a legal obligation, under California law. No specific California statute setting a response-time deadline or a writing requirement for reference requests was located during this research; that absence is reported honestly rather than assumed away. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1053); no additional independent source was found for this.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Prepared by:

_______________________________________________
On behalf of Acme, Inc.
Date: _______________
